papers.title: Utilization of Micro-Doppler Radar to Classify Gait Patterns of Young and Elderly Adults: An Approach Using a Long Short-Term Memory Network
papers.authors: Sora Hayashi, Kenshi Saho, Keitaro Shioiri, Masahiro Fujimoto, Masao Masugi
papers.venue: Sensors (Basel, Switzerland), MDPI — open access via PMC (PMC8197185)
papers.modality: Radar — micro-Doppler radar (MDR), 24 GHz continuous-wave (mono-static, ILT Office BSS-110)
papers.dataset: Self-collected (not public, withheld for privacy). Participants walked toward a fixed MDR along a ~10 m walkway at self-selected comfortable speed; radar mounted 0.86 m high; radar sampling frequency 600 Hz. No clothing restrictions. Two steady-state walking cycles per participant were used as the analysis interval. Notably, young and elderly data were collected at different locations (a stated confound).
papers.sample_size: 300 participants total: 87 young adults (mean age 22.0 +/- 1.7 yr; height 169.7 +/- 8.7 cm) and 213 elderly adults (mean age 72.5 +/- 4.8 yr; height 156.3 +/- 8.6 cm). Binary task: Young vs Elderly.
papers.methodology: 24 GHz CW radar (40 mW EIRP; -3 dB beamwidth 70 deg E-plane / 28 deg H-plane; coherent detection). STFT (Hamming window, 128 samples) produces time-velocity (micro-Doppler) spectrograms. Instead of feeding full spectrograms, they extract three velocity time-series from each spectrogram: upper envelope v_u(t) (max velocity, swing phase), lower envelope v_l(t) (min velocity, stance phase), and power-weighted mean envelope v_m(t) (torso). Peak-extraction threshold rho = 0.2 for denoising. These 1-D time-series feed an LSTM classifier: sequence input -> 1 LSTM layer (400 hidden units) -> fully connected -> softmax (Young/Elderly). Adam optimizer, initial LR 0.0001, batch size 128, LR decayed x0.9 every 30 epochs, zero-padding for uniform batch length. Several input conditions tested (combinations of the three envelopes). Validation: hold-out 7:3 split (210 train / 90 test), average accuracy over 30 random trials — NOT subject-independent LOSO.
papers.key_findings: Age-related gait differences (acceleration and stance-phase characteristics) are detectable from MDR leg-motion time-series. The lower envelope v_l(t) alone (stance/leg minimum velocity) gave the best classification, outperforming the upper and mean envelopes and their combinations. Feeding extracted envelope time-series to an LSTM captured comprehensive temporal information better than prior velocity-parameter/SVM methods. This is presented as the first radar-based method to exceed 90% accuracy on young/elderly gait classification.
papers.reported_performance: Proposed LSTM with lower-envelope input: overall accuracy 94.9% (young 91.7%, elderly 97.8%). Baselines/comparisons: previous velocity-parameter SVM method 85.7%; CNN (AlexNet) on spectrograms 97.8% — but authors caution the CNN result is likely unreliable/biased because it keyed on background-noise artifacts (young vs elderly recorded at different locations) rather than gait.
papers.pros: Contactless/remote sensing; no markers or wearables on the subject; unaffected by lighting and clothing; privacy-friendlier than video. Envelope-extraction preprocessing (peak threshold rho=0.2) suppresses background-noise artifacts, making the LSTM more robust than the raw-spectrogram CNN. Interpretable, physiologically grounded features (swing/stance/torso envelopes). Large sample (300) and strong reported accuracy (94.9%).
papers.cons_limitations: Young and elderly data were collected in different locations, giving group-dependent noise characteristics — a location/site confound. The authors themselves show the AlexNet CNN exploited this background-noise bias rather than gait, casting doubt on spectrogram-CNN results. Validation is hold-out 7:3 (30 random splits), not subject-independent LOSO, so numbers may be optimistic and subject leakage is not ruled out. The mechanism for why the lower envelope works best is not fully explained. Dataset is not public. Future work suggested: middle-aged subjects, larger datasets, fuzzy time-series methods.
papers.relevance_to_us: Very close modality match to our radar micro-Doppler Parkinson's work: same 24 GHz CW micro-Doppler gait spectrograms, same young-vs-elderly-style binary gait framing (here aging, ours PD). Two direct methodological contrasts: (1) they use an LSTM on extracted 1-D envelope time-series rather than a CNN on full spectrograms — a viable alternative/complement to our CNN; (2) they explicitly document a data-collection confound (young/elderly recorded at different sites) that biased their AlexNet CNN toward background noise, which is directly analogous to our duration/site confound concerns. Their validation is hold-out 7:3, not LOSO on 58 subjects like ours, so our LOSO protocol is more rigorous and our lower AUC (~0.62) is expected to be less inflated.
papers.lesson_for_us: Their own CNN-vs-LSTM comparison is a cautionary tale: a spectrogram CNN hit 97.8% but was flagged as unreliable because it latched onto site/background-noise differences between groups rather than gait — exactly the confound-leakage failure mode we are guarding against. This supports (a) preferring interpretable, denoised gait-specific features (envelope time-series) or at least verifying our CNN attends to gait not artifacts, and (b) using subject-independent LOSO instead of random hold-out to avoid inflated accuracy. Also worth testing: extracting upper/lower/mean Doppler envelopes and feeding a sequence model (LSTM) as a baseline against our CNN, and checking whether a stance-phase (lower-envelope) feature carries most of the PD signal.
papers.evidence_quote: We achieved a classification accuracy of 94.9%, which is significantly higher than that of a previously presented velocity-parameter-based classification method.

papers.title: Towards a Low-Cost Solution for Gait Analysis Using Millimeter Wave Sensor and Machine Learning
papers.authors: Mubarak A. Alanazi, Abdullah K. Alhazmi, Osama Alsattam, Kara Gnau, Meghan Brown, Shannon Thiel, Kurt Jackson, Vamsy P. Chodavarapu
papers.modality: Radar — Texas Instruments IWR6843ISK-ODS millimeter-wave (mmWave) FMCW radar, 60.75 GHz carrier, ~1780 MHz bandwidth, ~12 m max unambiguous range. Two data products used: micro-Doppler spectrograms and 5D point clouds (for skeletal pose).
papers.dataset: Self-collected in a laboratory under an IRB-approved clinical study at the University of Dayton. Three walking scenarios: perpendicular, parallel, and free (forward/backward) walking. Radar data converted to CSV with temporal/spatial measurements. Five simulated gait patterns: normal walking, limping, stooped posture, walking with a walker, walking with a cane. Kinect V2 used as ground truth for joint/pose validation.
papers.sample_size: Approximately 74 participants recruited (healthy subjects simulating gait patterns; not a Parkinson's patient cohort).
papers.methodology: Signal processing: FMCW chirp processing, range/velocity FFT, Moving Target Indication (MTI) clutter removal, CFAR detection, DBSCAN clustering, and Kalman-filter subject tracking for multi-person separation. Machine learning: a four-layer CNN (kernel/filter depths 32, 64, 128, 256; Leaky ReLU, 2D max-pooling, batch normalization, 5% dropout, softmax) classifies micro-Doppler signatures into the five gait patterns; a separate two-layer CNN regresses 3D skeletal joint positions (19 joints) from the 5D point cloud. Five models trained and averaged to reduce system error. Emphasis on a low-cost, plug-in, real-time, privacy-preserving alternative to cameras and battery-limited wearables.
papers.key_findings: The mmWave radar + CNN pipeline distinguished five gait patterns (normal, limping, stooped posture, walker, cane) with high accuracy and simultaneously reconstructed 3D skeletal pose in real time for multiple subjects. Assistive-device gaits (walker, cane) were classified most accurately, while overlapping gaits (normal, stooped, limping) were slightly harder to separate. Joint localization was accurate for large joints but degraded for wrist/hand joints due to radar range resolution. Authors position mmWave radar as a viable low-cost, contactless, privacy-preserving gait-monitoring solution for frailty/neurodegenerative-related abnormal gait.
papers.reported_performance: Gait-pattern classification accuracy: walking with walker 98.8%, walking with cane 98.4%, normal walking 97.2%, stooped posture ~96.5%, limping ~95.7% (last two derived from the confusion matrix). Skeletal joint localization (mean over 19 joints): MAE = 5.86 cm (x), 2.98 cm (y), 5.49 cm (z); RMSE = 8.66 cm (x), 4.45 cm (y), 7.75 cm (z). Computational: total inference 2.2–3.7 s for 50,400 frames; per-frame 54.3–92.5 microseconds; power 3900.2–5763.4 mW.
papers.pros: Uses low-cost, commercially available mmWave radar (contactless, works in low light, privacy-preserving vs. cameras, no battery burden vs. wearables); full pipeline from raw radar to both gait classification and 3D pose; real-time, multi-subject capability with explicit compute/power budgets; validated pose against Kinect V2 ground truth; high reported classification accuracy across five clinically motivated gait patterns.
papers.cons_limitations: Gait patterns are simulated by healthy participants, not real patients — no actual Parkinson's/clinical cohort, so it is gait-pattern recognition rather than disease diagnosis. Validation protocol is not clearly specified: no explicit subject-independent or leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) split is reported and the train/val/test ratio is undisclosed, so the high accuracies likely reflect frame/sample-level splitting that risks subject leakage and optimistic bias. Higher localization error for wrist/hand joints (mmWave ~0.084 m range resolution); overlapping gaits (normal/stooped/limping) reduce class separability; lab-only data, limited generalizability.
papers.relevance_to_us: Directly adjacent: it is a radar (mmWave micro-Doppler) + CNN gait-classification study, the same sensing-and-model family as our radar micro-Doppler PD CNN. It supports the premise that CNNs on radar micro-Doppler can discriminate abnormal gaits and explicitly cites stooped posture as characteristic of Parkinson's. However, it differs on the two axes we care most about: (1) it does NOT diagnose PD (healthy subjects mimic gaits) and (2) it does NOT use LOSO / subject-independent validation, whereas our work does LOSO on 58 real subjects. It is therefore a strong methodological citation but a weak/optimistic performance baseline — its ~95–99% accuracies are not comparable to our subject-independent AUCs.
papers.lesson_for_us: Frame-level or unspecified splits produce very high (95–99%) accuracies that are not trustworthy for clinical generalization; our LOSO-on-58-subjects protocol is more honest and explains why our numbers look lower. When citing this paper, use it to justify the mmWave-radar-micro-Doppler-CNN approach and the clinical motivation (stooped/abnormal gait in PD), but explicitly contrast validation rigor: emphasize subject-independent evaluation and the duration/confound controls we apply. Also note their radar-resolution limits on fine joints as motivation for our Doppler-domain feature choices.
papers.evidence_quote: "The proposed method attained the highest prediction accuracy of 98.8% for walking with a walker, closely followed by a prediction accuracy of 98.4% for walking with a cane."

papers.title: Comparative Analysis of Audio Processing Techniques on Doppler Radar Signature of Human Walking Motion Using CNN Models
papers.authors: Minh-Khue Ha, Thien-Luan Phan, Duc Hoang Ha Nguyen, Nguyen Hoang Quan, Ngoc-Quan Ha-Phan, Congo Tak Shing Ching, Nguyen Van Hieu
papers.modality: Radar (Doppler micro-Doppler). Continuous-wave K-Band radar at 24 GHz ISM band, using an InnoSenT IPS-354 K-Band transceiver.
papers.dataset: Self-collected CW Doppler radar dataset of human walking motion. Three motion classes: non-human motion, human normal walking, and human walking without arm swing. Subjects moved bidirectionally (toward/away from radar). Class distribution by duration: human walking without arms ~27 min, human normal walking ~25 min, non-human ~19 min (71 min total). No public/PD dataset used; not a clinical/Parkinson's dataset.
papers.sample_size: 6 subjects (5 male, 1 female; ages 22-25; height 1.5-1.75 m). 4,100 spectrogram samples total across ~71 minutes of recording.
papers.methodology: Comparative study of three "audio processing" time-frequency representations applied to raw radar returns: Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT), Mel spectrogram, and Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCC, 128 coefficients). STFT params: window length 1024, hop length 512 (50% overlap), FFT length 1024. These representations were fed to CNN classifiers: a 2D CNN (2 conv layers, 3x3 kernels, Tanh activation, 2x2 max-pooling, 0.1 dropout, dense + softmax), a 1D CNN (1D conv, batch norm, length-3 max-pooling, 0.3 dropout, dense-1024, softmax), and an ANN baseline (7 dense layers, ~1.41M weights, ReLU). Training: Adam optimizer, initial LR 1e-4, 200 epochs, batch size 32.
papers.key_findings: MFCC features gave the best and most generalizable representation because the cepstral transform removes global frequency shifts caused by varying walking speed, yielding features robust across speeds and to noise. The 2D CNN on MFCC outperformed all other feature/model combinations; mel-spectrogram was the weakest representation. Models were compact (~13 MB) with competitive inference times, supporting a low-cost, privacy-preserving radar surveillance use case.
papers.reported_performance: Best: 2D CNN + MFCC — 97.93% accuracy, 0.9807 precision, 0.9802 recall, 0.9805 F1, 0.9979 AUC. 1D CNN + MFCC — 97.44% accuracy, 0.9760 precision, 0.9760 F1. 2D CNN + STFT — 97.20% accuracy. 2D CNN + mel-spectrogram — 89.27% accuracy (weakest).
papers.pros: Directly compares three time-frequency (audio-derived) feature representations on the same radar data and CNN pipelines, isolating the effect of the front-end representation. Demonstrates MFCC's speed/noise robustness for micro-Doppler. Low-cost, privacy-preserving 24 GHz CW radar hardware. Compact models (~13 MB) suitable for deployment.
papers.cons_limitations: Very small cohort (only 6 young, healthy, similar-build participants) — explicitly noted by authors as a limitation. Task is coarse gait/motion classification (walking vs. no-arm-swing vs. non-human), not a clinical or Parkinson's diagnosis. Evaluation uses a random 72/8/20 train/val/test split with shuffling and NO subject-independent (LOSO) validation, so reported ~98% accuracy is likely optimistic due to same-subject samples leaking across splits. Limited to walking motions.
papers.relevance_to_us: Highly relevant as a methods/front-end reference for our radar micro-Doppler + CNN pipeline: it establishes that MFCC (over STFT and mel-spectrogram) is the strongest time-frequency representation for classifying gait-related micro-Doppler signatures, and that a small 2D CNN suffices. Directly informs feature-extraction choices for our PD classification. However, it is NOT a PD paper, has only 6 subjects vs. our 58, and — critically — uses random splitting rather than LOSO, so its ~98% numbers are not comparable to our subject-independent LOSO setting and serve as a cautionary contrast on evaluation rigor.
papers.lesson_for_us: (1) Consider adding MFCC/cepstral representations alongside our raw Doppler-time features — cepstral processing removes global speed-induced frequency shifts, a plausible confound-reducer worth testing against our duration/speed confound. (2) A compact 2D CNN can be competitive, so heavy architectures are not required. (3) Their headline ~98% accuracy comes from a random shuffled split with only 6 subjects; this reinforces why our LOSO-on-58-subjects protocol is the more honest, generalizable evaluation, and why cross-subject numbers (our AUC ~0.62) are far lower but more trustworthy.
papers.evidence_quote: "The experimental results demonstrated that the 2D CNN model trained on the MFCC feature outperformed the other two methods."

papers.title: Overview of Radar-Based Gait Parameter Estimation Techniques for Fall Risk Assessment
papers.authors: Sevgi Z. Gurbuz, Mohammad Mahbubur Rahman, Zahra Bassiri, Dario Martelli
papers.venue: IEEE Open Journal of Engineering in Medicine and Biology, Vol. 5, pp. 735-749. NOTE: The task described this as "Sensors (MDPI)", but the retrieved PMC record (PMC11342925) is the IEEE OJEMB paper — venue corrected to match actual source.
papers.modality: Radar (primary) — mmWave FMCW MIMO radar, Texas Instruments IWR2243 cascade, 77-81 GHz, 12 Tx / 16 Rx = 192 virtual channels. Compared against optical motion capture (8-camera Vicon, gold standard). Two radar data representations examined: micro-Doppler signatures and RF-derived skeletons.
papers.dataset: Original pilot study collected by the authors (radar + synchronized Vicon), plus a broad literature survey of prior radar gait/fall-risk datasets. No large public benchmark; the pilot is a small in-lab, single-session dataset.
papers.sample_size: Pilot study: 5 healthy male subjects (age 25.6 +/- 1.9 years, mass 70.6 +/- 17.5 kg); 5-minute self-paced walking trials on a 6 m walkway; ~5,600 radar frames per subject. Ground truth via 8-camera Vicon (100 Hz, 41 markers).
papers.methodology: Review/survey paper combined with an original experimental pilot. Surveys radar-based quantitative gait analysis (QGA) methods for fall risk. Experimentally compares three data representations for estimating gait parameters: (1) micro-Doppler (uD) signatures, (2) RF skeleton reconstructed from real radar (SkelR), and (3) RF skeleton from simulated data (SkelS). A 3D CNN + bidirectional LSTM DNN reconstructs 14 skeletal joints (42 coordinates). Gait parameters analyzed: step time (ST), step length (SL), step time variability (STV), step length variability (SLV). Agreement with Vicon assessed via mean percent difference and Bland-Altman limits of agreement; RF-skeleton accuracy via joint MAE.
papers.key_findings: Radar can estimate discrete gait parameters (step time, step length) with excellent agreement to optical motion capture, but gait variability measures (STV, SLV) — which are the most clinically informative for fall risk — show only poor-to-moderate agreement. RF-skeleton representations outperform raw micro-Doppler for step length (uD systematically underestimates SL by ~13%), while all methods do well on step time. Micro-Doppler captures whole-body aggregate backscatter (not per-joint), limiting fine spatial gait analysis. Deep-learning skeleton reconstruction introduces non-trivial estimation uncertainty from network design/training and is data-hungry.
papers.reported_performance: Step time mean difference: uD 1.00% +/- 1.71%; SkelR -0.54% +/- 1.09%; SkelS -0.12% +/- 0.76% (all excellent agreement). Step length mean difference: uD -13.03% +/- 4.52% (good, underestimates); SkelR 1.84% +/- 1.05%; SkelS 0.90% +/- 0.72% (both excellent, ~1-2% error). RF-skeleton joint MAE (simulated): ML 3.15 cm, Vertical 4.37 cm, AP 1.4 cm; (real radar): ML 5.63 cm, Vertical 7.30 cm, AP 7.81 cm. Variability: STV poor-to-moderate (>50% limits of agreement), SLV moderate (10-50%). Cited lit: walking-speed validation error 0.076 m/s.
papers.pros: Comprehensive, well-organized survey of radar QGA methods paired with a gold-standard (Vicon) validated pilot. Directly quantifies the accuracy gap between micro-Doppler and RF-skeleton representations. Highlights radar's non-intrusive, privacy-preserving, contactless nature suitable for continuous in-home monitoring without subject burden. Simulated-vs-real comparison usefully isolates DNN-induced uncertainty.
papers.cons_limitations: Very small pilot (n=5, all healthy young males) — no fall-prone or clinical population, limiting external validity. Radar ran at only 10 Hz vs Vicon 100 Hz; poor elevation angular resolution (4 active elevation channels). Gait variability — the most fall-relevant metric — has poor/moderate agreement (up to ~100% overestimation). Micro-Doppler cannot isolate individual joints/body parts. Deep-learning methods are "data greedy" and carry estimation uncertainty. Multi-person disambiguation, obstacles, motion artifacts, and real-world clutter are not addressed; validation limited to controlled indoor lab. Kinect (often used as ground truth in cited work) is criticized as inadequate.
papers.relevance_to_us: Highly relevant to a radar micro-Doppler PD CNN with LOSO on 58 subjects. It is the leading survey framing of the micro-Doppler-vs-skeleton tradeoff and validates that micro-Doppler alone captures only whole-body aggregate motion — reinforcing why our per-subject signal is weak-but-real rather than cleanly joint-specific. It confirms micro-Doppler's strength on step-time-like temporal features and its weakness on spatial/variability features, and it establishes radar as a credible clinical gait modality. Our study is larger (58 vs 5) and disease-classification-focused (PD) rather than parameter-estimation, and uses proper subject-independent LOSO — a methodological strength over this small single-session pilot.
papers.lesson_for_us: Gait variability/complexity features are the most clinically discriminative for gait pathology but are also the hardest to estimate reliably from radar — expect noise there, and be cautious about energy/duration-driven artifacts (mirrors our duration confound). Micro-Doppler = whole-body aggregate, so don't over-interpret features as joint-specific. Larger subject counts and rigorous subject-independent evaluation (our LOSO on 58) are exactly what this field's small pilots lack, strengthening our contribution. Consider positioning micro-Doppler CNN results against the known uD limitations (SL underestimation, variability instability) this paper documents.
papers.evidence_quote: While there is excellent agreement between radar and optical tracking estimates of step time and step length, gait variability measures show poor to moderate agreement.

papers.title: STRIDE: Systematic Radar Intelligence Analysis for ADRD Risk Evaluation with Gait Signature Simulation and Deep Learning
papers.authors: Fulin Cai, Abhidnya Patharkar, Teresa Wu, Fleming Y. M. Lure, Harry Chen, Victor C. Chen
papers.venue: IEEE Sensors Journal, vol. 23, no. 10, pp. 10998–11006 (open access via PMC; PMC10399976)
papers.modality: Radar — micro-Doppler radar (non-wearable). Simulated radar: 1.5 GHz bandwidth, 1.0 ms sweep time, 512 grouped sweeps, 0.1 m range resolution.
papers.dataset: Fully SIMULATED "digital-twin" gait-signature dataset. Two coupled simulators: (1) a human-walking model driven by established biomechanical walking parameters that synthesizes ADRD-affected gaits under varied conditions, and (2) a micro-Doppler radar model based on electromagnetic scattering + Doppler frequency-shift theory that generates signatures from moving body parts (foot, limb, joint, torso, shoulder, etc.). No real/human data collected.
papers.sample_size: No real subjects (0 human participants). 8,000 simulated walking samples total: 2,000 per class across 4 ADRD-risk severity categories (Normal, Subtle, Moderate, Severe Abnormality).
papers.methodology: Pipeline: simulate gait -> generate micro-Doppler radar returns -> STFT spectrogram (512 DFT points, 256-sample overlap, 256-point Kaiser window; ~512 x 776 frequency-by-time spectrogram) -> deep-learning classification. Core method is a Band-Dependent Learning (BDL) framework: the spectrogram is split into N non-overlapping frequency sub-bands, each processed and assigned a learned importance weight (sigmoid-mapped to [0,1]) to down-weight noisy/uninformative bands, integrated on a ResNet-18 backbone (BDL-ResNet) yielding a 512-d feature vector into a 512x4 FC classifier (ReLU, batch norm). Training: Adam, lr 1e-3, batch size 64, cross-entropy loss, early stopping, up to 5 epochs. Evaluation: random 70%/15%/15% train/val/test split, repeated 30 times with re-splitting and re-initialization (NOT subject-independent / not LOSO — samples are simulated). Baselines: ResNet-18, GoogleNet, SVM, NN.
papers.key_findings: Micro-Doppler radar plus a band-dependent deep classifier can distinguish four levels of ADRD-related gait abnormality on simulated data. The BDL-ResNet, which learns per-frequency-band importance weights, significantly outperforms standard CNNs and classical ML baselines. Best and worst separability are at the extremes (Normal, Severe) while the intermediate Subtle/Moderate classes are hardest. Authors frame abnormal gait as a non-cognitive biomarker detectable up to ~10 years before ADRD clinical symptoms.
papers.reported_performance: Overall accuracy (mean +/- std over 30 runs): BDL-ResNet 0.923 +/- 0.018; GoogleNet 0.905 +/- 0.013; SVM 0.898 +/- 0.007; ResNet-18 0.884 +/- 0.078; NN 0.740 +/- 0.007. Per-class BDL-ResNet: Normal precision 0.977, sensitivity 0.996; Subtle precision 0.822, sensitivity 0.902; Moderate precision 0.920, sensitivity 0.794; Severe precision 0.995, sensitivity 0.997. Authors state "BDL-ResNet significantly outperforms the other algorithms in terms of overall accuracy with at least 95% confidence."
papers.pros: Non-wearable and privacy-preserving relative to cameras and wearables. Introduces a novel, interpretable band-dependent weighting mechanism that reduces the impact of variability/noise across frequency bands and beats standard CNN and classical baselines. Digital-twin simulation allows controlled generation of graded gait-abnormality severity and large balanced datasets without recruiting patients. Repeated (30x) cross-validation gives variance estimates.
papers.cons_limitations: Results are entirely on SIMULATED data — no real radar or human validation, so the high accuracy is optimistic and not directly comparable to real-world performance. Simulation is a near-empty room with only channel noise (unrealistic); lacks clutter and multiple subjects. Human walking model is not elderly-specific (no humpback/tremor). Evaluation uses random sample splits, NOT subject-independent (no LOSO), so generalization across individuals is untested. Intermediate severity classes (Subtle/Moderate) are hard to separate. Authors acknowledge need for field testing and transfer learning to adapt to real data. Targets ADRD/dementia gait severity, not Parkinson's specifically.
papers.relevance_to_us: Directly adjacent: same modality (micro-Doppler radar) and same broad approach (spectrogram + CNN/ResNet) for neurodegenerative gait classification, but a strong methodological CONTRAST to our setup. We use REAL data from 58 subjects with subject-independent LOSO for Parkinson's; STRIDE uses zero real subjects, purely simulated data, and random (subject-mixing) splits, which likely inflates its 0.923 accuracy versus our ~0.62 LOSO AUC. Their band-dependent (per-frequency sub-band) weighting is a concrete, transferable architectural idea we could test on our real spectrograms, especially given our 5 Hz Doppler-bin structure. Useful as a "simulation upper-bound / idealized" reference point and to justify why real-subject LOSO numbers are far lower and more honest.
papers.lesson_for_us: (1) Accuracy on simulated or subject-mixed data is not comparable to real-subject LOSO — cite STRIDE as the idealized ceiling and frame our lower LOSO AUC as the realistic, generalizable number. (2) The band-dependent weighting idea (learn per-frequency-sub-band importance, sigmoid-gated) is worth prototyping on our real micro-Doppler to suppress noisy bins. (3) Their own limitations (empty-room, no clutter, no elderly model, need for transfer learning and field testing) validate the value of our real-world dataset and motivate confound controls; also note the graded-severity framing (4 abnormality levels) as an alternative to binary PD-vs-control labeling.
papers.evidence_quote: Abnormal gait is a significant non-cognitive biomarker for Alzheimer's disease (AD) and AD-related dementia (ADRD). Micro-Doppler radar, a non-wearable technology, can capture human gait movements for potential early ADRD risk assessment. ... As a proof of concept, we develop a "digital-twin" of STRIDE, consisting of a human walking simulation model and a micro-Doppler radar simulation model, to generate a gait signature dataset.

papers.title: Deep Learning-based identification of human gait by radar micro-Doppler measurements
papers.authors: Conference paper (IEEE EuRAD 2020): V. S. Papanastasiou, R. P. Trommel, R. I. A. Harmanny, A. Yarovoy. The IEEE page itself was blocked/empty; content was retrieved from the open-access TU Delft MSc thesis version of the same work, authored by Vasileios Papanastasiou (TU Delft, EEMCS).
papers.year: 2020 (IEEE EuRAD conference paper); underlying MSc thesis dated 2019.
papers.venue: 2020 17th European Radar Conference (EuRAD), IEEE. Open-access source used: MSc Thesis, Delft University of Technology (TU Delft Repository, uuid:4a1ea237-2857-4c26-aad5-1f523fdde58a).
papers.modality: Radar — continuous-wave (CW) X-band radar micro-Doppler (m-D) signatures / spectrograms of walking humans.
papers.dataset: Micro-Doppler measurements of subjects walking toward and away from the radar, plus complementary simulated m-D data. Not a public benchmark; collected by the authors (TU Delft / partner). Radar: CW X-band.
papers.sample_size: 22 subjects (closed-set / cohort of 22 participants). Supplemented with simulated gait data.
papers.methodology: Pipeline over micro-Doppler spectrograms: (1) unsupervised representation learning with Adversarial Autoencoders to map m-D signatures into a latent space; (2) t-SNE and UMAP for clustering and visualization/interpretation of the latent space; (3) supervised identification with a VGG-16 deep convolutional neural network (DCNN) classifying subjects from their measured m-D signature. Study also analyzes how gait characteristics (walking speed, stride, gender) shape distinctive m-D signatures, using both simulated and measured data.
papers.key_findings: Demonstrates (reportedly for the first time at X-band) that individual human walking gait produces distinctive radar micro-Doppler signatures usable for personnel identification via DCNNs. Even very slight differences in gait characteristics (speed, stride, gender) map to closely located points in the learned latent space, so individuals are separable. UMAP/t-SNE confirm cluster structure by subject. A VGG-16 CNN successfully identifies the 22 walking subjects from their m-D signatures.
papers.reported_performance: "Accuracy of above 93.5% was achieved" for identification across the 22-subject population (VGG-16 classifier on measured m-D signatures). No AUC, per-subject precision/recall, or open-set metrics reported in the retrieved abstract.
papers.pros: First demonstration of human identification (not just activity classification) from CW X-band micro-Doppler using deep CNNs; combines unsupervised representation learning (Adversarial Autoencoder) with strong visualization/interpretability (UMAP, t-SNE) to explain why identities separate; uses both simulated and real measured data; high reported closed-set accuracy (>93.5%); establishes that fine gait mechanics are encoded in m-D signatures.
papers.cons_limitations: Small cohort (only 22 subjects) — authors explicitly note reliability is "for 22 participants"; task is closed-set cohort classification (identity), not open-set recognition and not a clinical/pathological task; constrained walking geometry (toward/away from radar, i.e., near-radial aspect) limits aspect-angle robustness; no explicit subject-independent (LOSO) or cross-session/cross-day protocol described in retrieved content, so the reported accuracy likely reflects within-cohort splits and may be optimistic; no confidence intervals or per-class breakdown reported.
papers.relevance_to_us: Highly relevant methodologically and as a confound warning. Same modality (radar micro-Doppler spectrograms), same core approach (CNN, here VGG-16) on human gait — directly comparable pipeline to our radar m-D PD CNN. Critically, it shows individual identity is strongly and separably encoded in m-D signatures (>93.5% ID accuracy on 22 people). For our PD-vs-control classification on 58 subjects, this means subject identity is a major leakage risk: any train/test split that shares subjects can let the model classify PD by memorizing individuals rather than pathology — which is exactly why our LOSO (subject-independent) protocol is the right, more honest choice. Their UMAP-based latent inspection is a technique we can reuse to check whether our embeddings cluster by subject/identity (confound) versus by PD label. Note our task and evaluation are harder and not directly comparable to their 93.5%.
papers.lesson_for_us: (1) Because individual gait is highly identifiable in micro-Doppler, subject-independent evaluation (LOSO) is essential — within-cohort splits inflate accuracy via identity leakage, so their 93.5% is not a fair benchmark for our LOSO AUC. (2) Small cohorts (22 here) yield optimistic numbers; our 58-subject LOSO will read lower but is more trustworthy — frame it that way. (3) Adopt UMAP/t-SNE to visually audit whether learned features separate by PD status or merely by subject identity/duration confounds (cf. our duration-confound and weak-but-real signal findings). (4) VGG-style CNNs on m-D spectrograms and CW X-band data are a validated, sufficient baseline architecture/setup. (5) Controlled radial walking geometry aids performance but limits generalization — worth noting when comparing to freer clinical gait.
papers.evidence_quote: Accuracy of above 93.5% was achieved, proving that CW X-band radar m-D signature of human walking gait can be used for accurate personnel identification which is reliable for 22 participants.

papers.title: Doppler Radar for the Extraction of Biomechanical Parameters in Gait Analysis
papers.authors: Ann-Kathrin Seifert; Martin Grimmer; Abdelhak M. Zoubir (Signal Processing Group and Institute of Sports Science, Technische Universitat Darmstadt, Germany)
papers.venue: arXiv preprint, arXiv:2005.05280v1 [eess.SP], 11 May 2020 (open access). Carries an IEEE 2020 copyright notice; the accepted/published version appeared in IEEE Journal of Biomedical and Health Informatics (J-BHI).
papers.modality: Radar. Specifically a 24 GHz continuous-wave (CW) mono-static Doppler radar (Ancortek SDR-KIT 2400AD), micro-Doppler signature analysis. Validated against two gold-standard reference modalities: marker-based 3D motion capture (Qualisys, 12 infrared cameras, 500 Hz) and ground reaction forces (GRF) from an instrumented treadmill.
papers.dataset: Authors' own purpose-collected experimental dataset (no public/named dataset). Simultaneous recordings of radar micro-Doppler, mocap, and GRF while subjects walked on an instrumented treadmill. Radar placed at ~knee height (0.58 m above treadmill), 1.75 m in front of or behind the subject, 0-degree to line-of-sight; only one radar active at a time. Conditions: two speeds (0.7 m/s "slow", 1.1 m/s "fast"), five right-knee-flexion restrictions via an adjustable orthosis (none/normal, 45, 30, 20, 10 degrees) to simulate asymmetric/abnormal gait, and two radar views (front/back). ~100 s of walking analyzed per speed after trimming.
papers.sample_size: 19 able-bodied volunteers with no gait impairment (5 female, 14 male; age 28.9 +/- 7.5 years; height 176.5 +/- 10.2 cm; mass 72.3 +/- 11.5 kg). Note: only 18 samples available for the normal-walking and 45-degree conditions due to mocap/GRF synchronization errors. Ethics approval EK 31/2018; written consent obtained.
papers.methodology: This is a signal-processing validation/measurement study, NOT a machine-learning classification study. Pipeline: CW radar return -> STFT spectrogram (Hamming window M=256, 255-sample overlap, zero-padded to 2048 points; ~40 Hz / 0.25 m/s frequency resolution, 0.1 s time resolution; data sampled at 12.8 kHz, sub-sampled to 2.56 kHz) -> adaptive noise thresholding -> morphological operations (dilation/erosion, hole filling, small-component removal) to extract micro-Doppler envelope signals. Novel contributions: (1) new methods to extract sagittal velocities of individual lower-limb joints (toe, ankle, knee) by using proportionally different noise thresholds (e.g., knee at 55% of adaptive threshold, ankle at 75-85%, toe at 85%), and (2) a new method to extract individual-leg flight (swing) time from radar by using the time instant of maximal knee velocity as a proxy for the toe-off event. Gait cycles segmented from envelope minima; 11 gait parameters extracted (stride/stance/flight/step time, cadence, stride/step length, maximal toe/ankle/knee velocity, and time instant of maximal knee velocity). Radar vs mocap agreement tested with the Wilcoxon signed-rank test (paired, two-sided, alpha=0.05) across 220 tests, with Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate correction. Radar and mocap were time-synchronized via generalized cross-correlation of envelopes; a mean sampling-drift of 0.01 s/sample was corrected.
papers.key_findings: Doppler radar can accurately measure many medically relevant gait parameters versus mocap+GRF. Five spatiotemporal parameters (stride time, step time, cadence, stride length, step length) were reliably extracted with near-zero differences across all speeds and both radar views. Three kinematic parameters (maximal toe, ankle, knee velocity) were accurately measured in most conditions, and radar captured the decrease in maximal knee velocity as the orthosis increasingly restricted the knee. Stance and flight time depend on correctly detecting the time instant of maximal knee velocity: this is reliably detected with a back view but underestimated with a front view (because the knee's signature is obscured by higher-energy upper-leg backscatter). Authors conclude radar is a viable contactless, privacy-preserving supplement for unobtrusive in-home gait analysis.
papers.reported_performance: Kinematic velocities (toe/ankle/knee) measured by radar agreed with mocap in 51 of 60 analyzed cases (85%). Toe and ankle velocities were incorrectly extracted in 2 of 20 scenarios; knee velocity in 5 of 20. Kinematic median differences were < 0.3 m/s. For the flight-time method, the average difference between the time instant of maximal knee velocity and the GRF toe-off time ranged 13-40 ms; given mean flight times of 448 ms (0.7 m/s) and 402 ms (1.1 m/s), maximal expected flight-time error was ~9% (0.7 m/s) and ~8% (1.1 m/s). Benjamini-Hochberg significance threshold p* = 0.0057. Cadence, stride length, and step length matched almost exactly (e.g., Table II radar vs mocap cadence agree to ~0.01-0.02 steps/min). Stance/flight time reliable for all conditions at 0.7 m/s; at 1.1 m/s reliable with back view (except unconstrained gait) but difficult with front view.
papers.pros: Contactless, privacy-preserving, unobtrusive, no user instrumentation - well suited for continuous in-home monitoring. Rigorously validated against gold-standard mocap AND GRF simultaneously (most prior radar-gait work only qualitatively compared). Introduces new, physically-motivated methods to extract individual lower-limb joint velocities and per-leg flight time from micro-Doppler. Demonstrates radar can sense small, induced changes in gait (orthosis), relevant to tracking relative disease progression. Sound statistics (Wilcoxon signed-rank + FDR control across 220 tests).
papers.cons_limitations: Small sample (19), all young, able-bodied adults - no clinical or elderly population; gait abnormality only simulated via a knee orthosis rather than real pathology. Treadmill-only data, not real overground/in-home walking. Front-view radar underestimates the time instant of maximal knee velocity, degrading stance/flight-time accuracy; knee velocity obscured by higher-energy upper-leg backscatter. Envelope-extraction thresholds were tuned empirically and depend on subject stature, multipath, and transmit power. Authors state absolute values are "not sufficiently accurate for professional gait analysis (yet)." Only one axis of impairment (knee flexion) studied; asymmetry measures only suggested, not implemented.
papers.relevance_to_us: Highly relevant as a methodological/foundational reference, though it is NOT a Parkinson's classifier and uses no CNN or LOSO. It shares our exact core modality (24 GHz Doppler radar micro-Doppler of gait) and directly establishes WHICH biomechanical gait parameters radar can and cannot reliably measure - the physical basis for any downstream PD classifier. Parkinson's disease is cited only as motivation in the intro/references, not studied. The paper explicitly contrasts its hand-crafted feature-extraction approach with "automatic data-driven feature learning using e.g. neural networks" and lists deep learning that maps micro-Doppler stride representations to biomechanical parameters as future work - i.e., it frames exactly the deep-learning gap our CNN approach fills. Its speed- and view-dependence findings also connect to our duration/energy confound concerns.
papers.lesson_for_us: (1) Radar micro-Doppler reliably captures spatiotemporal rhythm/pace parameters (stride/step time, cadence, stride/step length) but kinematic joint velocities and event timing are geometry-dependent - back view beats front view; this argues for controlling/reporting radar geometry and being cautious about knee-derived features. (2) Walking speed strongly affects the signatures and error rates, reinforcing that speed/duration are confounds to normalize (matches our duration-confound memory). (3) Validating on 19 young able-bodied treadmill subjects was explicitly flagged as insufficient - the authors call for "a larger clinical population," which supports the value of our 58-subject PD cohort. (4) They point to deep learning as the way to learn the micro-Doppler-to-gait-parameter mapping without hand-tuned thresholds, supporting our CNN over classical feature engineering. (5) Practical STFT settings (Hamming, heavy overlap, zero-padding) and the finer-than-intrinsic frequency grid mirror our own bin-spacing note.
papers.evidence_quote: "Based on radar data, five spatiotemporal parameters related to rhythm and pace could reliably be extracted. Further, for most of the considered conditions, three kinematic parameters could accurately be measured. ... For different knee angle confinements, the velocities measured by the radar system agree with those obtained using motion capturing in 51 out of the 60 analyzed cases (85%)."

papers.title: Lightweight FMCW radar framework for human activity recognition under limited data conditions
papers.authors: Ali Samimi Fard, Mohammadreza Mashhadigholamali, Samaneh Zolfaghari, Hajar Abedi, Mainak Chakraborty, Luigi Borzì, Masoud Daneshtalab, George Shaker
papers.venue: Scientific Reports (Nature), Volume 16, Article 9650, published 22 March 2026
papers.modality: Radar (60 GHz FMCW millimeter-wave radar). Not wearable/video.
papers.dataset: Newly collected 60 GHz FMCW mmWave radar dataset recorded in a realistic home-like bedroom environment. Seven activity classes: Walking, Sitting on Bed, Sitting on Chair, Lying on Bed, Lying on Floor, Empty Room, and Transition. The framework also reports a reduced 4-activity setting.
papers.sample_size: Very small subject pool: 3 healthy participants across 16 recording sessions, 7 activity classes. (No older adults / no patients; this is a healthy-only ADL dataset.)
papers.methodology: Lightweight deep learning pipeline. Signal processing: Blackman-Harris windowing, Range-FFT, Moving Target Indicator (MTI) clutter filtering to produce Range-Doppler maps, and Capon beamforming to extract Range-Azimuth and Range-Elevation maps. The three map types are fed as structured multi-dimensional data vectors (not as conventional 2D images). Model: a modified ResNet-18 backbone using depthwise separable convolutions (to cut complexity) followed by a bidirectional LSTM for spatio-temporal feature extraction. Data augmentation for the limited-data regime: spatial shifting, intensity scaling with bias shift, horizontal Doppler flipping, and additive Gaussian noise. Validation: Cross-Scene Validation (80/20 split across 14 scenes) and Leave-One-Person-Out (LOPO/LOSO) cross-validation. Reported model footprint: 0.814M parameters, 6.66 MB model size, 0.0696 GFLOPS.
papers.key_findings: Fusing Range-Doppler + Range-Azimuth + Range-Elevation feature maps outperformed single-map inputs. Treating radar maps as structured multi-dimensional vectors rather than 2D images, combined with a lightweight depthwise-separable ResNet-18 + BiLSTM, preserved accuracy while sharply reducing model complexity, making the model edge-deployable. The tailored radar-specific data augmentation substantially improved generalization under limited training data. Performance dropped notably from cross-scene to subject-independent (LOSO) evaluation, especially in F1, showing subject-independent generalization is harder.
papers.reported_performance: Cross-Scene, 7 activities: 91.98% accuracy, 89.82% F1. Cross-Scene, 4 activities: 98.62% accuracy, 98.70% F1. Leave-One-Person-Out, 7 activities: 89.74% accuracy, 83.24% F1. Leave-One-Person-Out, 4 activities: 94.47% accuracy, 85.86% F1. Model: 0.814M parameters, 6.66 MB, 0.0696 GFLOPS.
papers.pros: Privacy-preserving and unobtrusive (radar, no camera); explicitly targets limited-data / edge-device deployment with a very small model (0.814M params, ~6.7 MB, sub-0.07 GFLOPS); reports subject-independent (LOPO/LOSO) results, not just random splits; radar-specific augmentation recipe (Doppler flip, intensity scaling+bias, spatial shift, Gaussian noise) is concrete and reusable; preserves the physical meaning of radar axes by using structured map inputs; multi-view fusion (Doppler + azimuth + elevation) is well-motivated and shown to help.
papers.cons_limitations: Only 3 participants — so the LOSO result rests on training on 2 people and testing on 1, giving weak evidence of true subject-independent generalization; all participants healthy (no clinical population); few and coarse activity types; small home-like scene diversity; no on-device latency/power measurement despite the edge-deployment claim; authors flag the need to expand dataset diversity and explore transfer learning.
papers.relevance_to_us: Directly relevant methodologically to a radar micro-Doppler Parkinson's CNN with LOSO on 58 subjects. Same sensing family (FMCW mmWave, Range-Doppler / micro-Doppler maps) and same core problem (deep learning under limited radar data). It validates our design choices: a lightweight CNN backbone (depthwise-separable ResNet-18) + temporal module (BiLSTM), radar-specific data augmentation, and subject-independent LOSO evaluation. Notably one author (Luigi Borzì) works on Parkinson's gait, and the pipeline (RD maps -> lightweight CNN -> LOSO) mirrors ours. Their 91.98% cross-scene vs 89.74%/83.24% (acc/F1) LOSO gap is a useful comparator for framing the difficulty of subject-independent radar classification.
papers.lesson_for_us: Three takeaways. (1) Report and emphasize LOSO F1, not just accuracy: their F1 fell from 89.82% (cross-scene) to 83.24% (LOSO), a larger drop than accuracy, showing subject-independent generalization exposes weaknesses that pooled splits hide — reinforces our confound-controlled, subject-independent framing. (2) Their radar-specific augmentation set (horizontal Doppler flipping, intensity scaling with bias shift, spatial/temporal shifting, additive Gaussian noise) is directly portable to our micro-Doppler spectrograms and could raise our weak-but-real signal (LOSO AUC ~0.62). (3) A cautionary contrast: their headline LOSO rests on only 3 subjects, so it barely tests person-independence — our 58-subject LOSO is a genuine strength worth foregrounding, and beating a shallow n=3 generalization claim is not the bar; robustness across 58 subjects is.
papers.evidence_quote: The framework processes radar-derived Range-Doppler, Range-Azimuth, and Range-Elevation feature maps as structured multi-dimensional data vectors rather than conventional 2D images

papers.title: DNN Transfer Learning from Diversified Micro-Doppler for Motion Classification
papers.authors: Mehmet Saygin Seyfioglu, Baris Erol, Sevgi Zubeyde Gurbuz, Moeness G. Amin
papers.venue: arXiv preprint (1811.08361); accepted to IEEE Transactions on Aerospace and Electronic Systems (Nov 2018)
papers.modality: Radar micro-Doppler. Real target data from a 4-GHz continuous-wave (CW) software-defined radar; synthetic training data generated from Kinect-based MOCAP simulations.
papers.dataset: Two-part: (1) Synthetic source domain — 32,000 diversified micro-Doppler spectrograms generated from 55 original Kinect MOCAP measurements of 5 subjects. (2) Real target domain — measured 4-GHz CW radar micro-Doppler signatures of human activities/gaits collected indoors at TOBB University. Gait-relevant classes include walking, jogging, limping, walking with a cane, walking with a walker, falling, sitting (plus additional classes in the 11-class task).
papers.sample_size: 5 subjects for the Kinect MOCAP simulations (55 base recordings expanded to 32,000 synthetic samples via diversification). Measured radar set ~594 signatures for the 7-class task (walking 71, jogging 72, limping 104, cane 123, walker 121, falling 53, sitting 50); split into ~474 fine-tuning and ~120 test signatures. Exact number of real measured subjects not stated in the retrieved text.
papers.methodology: Proposes "DivNet": a 32-layer residual CNN (DivNet-15, 15 conv layers in 7 residual units, batch norm, pre-activation residual units). Central idea is transfer learning from a DOMAIN-MATCHED synthetic source rather than optical imagery. Kinect MOCAP skeletons are diversified via (a) scaling z-axis (height) and x-axis (speed) with leg-length/velocity kinematic coupling, (b) motion-speed variation via the Boulic-Thalmann model, and (c) Fourier-series modeling of joint trajectories with ~10% parameter perturbation, producing 32,000 physically plausible micro-Doppler signatures. The network is pre-trained on this diversified synthetic data, then fine-tuned on measured radar signatures. Evaluated on 7-class and 11-class human motion recognition and compared against ImageNet-pretrained VGGnet and ResNet-50, and a baseline CNN trained on measured data only.
papers.key_findings: Diversifying a small MOCAP set into a large synthetic micro-Doppler dataset lets a deep residual net be trained/pre-trained without a large real RF corpus. Transfer learning from domain-matched synthetic micro-Doppler outperforms transfer learning from optical imagery (VGGnet/ResNet-50) and a measured-data-only baseline. The approach yields robust performance on previously unseen target profiles and enables class generalization. DivNet also showed better bottleneck-feature quality and noise robustness at 40 dB SNR.
papers.reported_performance: 7-class: DivNet-15 "97%" test / "98%" validation; VGGnet transfer "94%"; ResNet-50 transfer "95%"; baseline CNN (measured only) "86%". 11-class: DivNet-15 "95.7%" test / "96%" validation; VGGnet "91%"; ResNet-50 "91%"; baseline CNN "87%". Noise robustness at 40 dB SNR: DivNet-15 "97%", ResNet-50 "95%", VGGnet "94%". Bottleneck features (7-class): DivNet-15 ~30% improvement and ResNet-50 ~15% improvement over VGGnet.
papers.pros: Directly tackles the small-radar-dataset problem that plagues micro-Doppler deep learning; physics-informed data augmentation (kinematically constrained MOCAP diversification) rather than naive image augmentation; demonstrates domain-matched pretraining beats ImageNet transfer, a clean and reusable result; tests generalization to unseen subjects/profiles and noise robustness; deep residual architecture appropriate for small data.
papers.cons_limitations: Not a Parkinson's/clinical study — classes are general activities and simulated gait aids (cane, walker, limping), not neurodegenerative gait. Only 5 subjects underlie all synthetic data, so kinematic diversity is bounded by a tiny seed set. Number of real measured subjects is unclear, and the train/test split appears sample-level rather than a strict leave-one-subject-out protocol, so cross-subject generalization claims are weaker than a formal LOSO would give. Synthetic-to-real domain gap and reliance on Kinect fidelity. Results are single-lab (TOBB), single-radar (4-GHz CW).
papers.relevance_to_us: Highly relevant. It is a radar micro-Doppler + CNN pipeline on gait-type motions, the same modality and model family as our radar micro-Doppler PD CNN with LOSO on 58 subjects. Its core problem — too few subjects/samples for deep learning — is exactly our constraint, and it offers a concrete, physics-based augmentation recipe (MOCAP diversification -> synthetic spectrograms) and evidence that domain-matched pretraining beats ImageNet transfer, both directly applicable to boosting our PD classifier. Limping/cane/walker classes are the closest available analogues to pathological gait.
papers.lesson_for_us: When labeled radar data is scarce, pretrain on domain-matched synthetic micro-Doppler (e.g., MOCAP-driven simulated PD vs. healthy gait) instead of ImageNet — the paper shows this gives large gains (e.g., 86% baseline -> 97% with diversified transfer on 7-class). Physically constrained diversification (height/speed/Fourier-gait perturbation) is a principled augmentation we can adapt. Caveat: their split is not strict LOSO, so our LOSO-on-58 design is methodologically stronger for cross-subject claims; we should report LOSO explicitly and be cautious that headline accuracies like theirs may be optimistic without subject-disjoint evaluation.
papers.evidence_quote: enables not only robust performance for previously unseen target profiles, but also class generalization ... offers improved performance in comparison to transfer learning from optical imagery

papers.title: Human identification based on natural gait micro-Doppler signatures using deep transfer learning
papers.venue: IET Radar, Sonar & Navigation, Vol. 14, Issue 10, pp. 1640-1646
papers.modality: Radar (frequency-modulated continuous-wave / FMCW radar micro-Doppler signatures)
papers.dataset: Authors' own gait micro-Doppler dataset collected with an FMCW radar sensor in an indoor environment. Each subject walked "naturally and freely" (unconstrained walking behaviour) rather than along a fixed constrained path, which the authors emphasize as more realistic and challenging than prior work. (Radar centre frequency, bandwidth, and dataset size in samples/spectrograms are not stated in the retrievable abstract; the full text is paywalled.)
papers.sample_size: 20 subjects/persons. Total number of micro-Doppler samples/spectrograms not available in the retrieved abstract.
papers.methodology: Closed-set gait-based human identification from radar micro-Doppler (m-D) signatures. FMCW radar returns are processed into m-D spectrogram images. Identification is performed with a ResNet-50 CNN pre-trained (ImageNet-style) and fine-tuned on the gait m-D dataset via deep transfer learning. The authors experimentally determined the optimal observation-window length of the m-D samples and used that as the network input. (Exact preprocessing parameters, train/test split ratio, and validation scheme are not in the retrievable abstract.)
papers.key_findings: 1) A ResNet-50 fine-tuned by transfer learning can identify individuals from radar micro-Doppler gait signatures under unconstrained/natural walking. 2) The observation-window length of m-D samples is a key hyperparameter; an optimal length was determined experimentally and materially affects accuracy. 3) With the optimal window, the method reached 96.7% average identification accuracy over 20 subjects, which the authors state outperforms state-of-the-art methods. 4) Demonstrates feasibility of a simple, cost-efficient radar device for automatic person identification by gait.
papers.reported_performance: "they achieved an average identification accuracy of 96.7% on the test set for 20 subjects, which highly outperforms the state-of-the-art methods." (Per-class/per-subject metrics, precision/recall, and confusion matrix are in the paywalled full text and were not retrieved.)
papers.pros: Uses natural, free/unconstrained walking rather than a fixed constrained gait path, making the task more realistic. Applies transfer learning (fine-tuned ResNet-50) which mitigates limited-data problems typical of radar datasets. High reported accuracy (96.7%). Uses a simple, low-cost FMCW radar, supporting practical deployment. Systematically tunes the observation-window length rather than assuming it.
papers.cons_limitations: Small cohort (only 20 subjects). Task is closed-set identification of healthy individuals, not clinical/pathological gait classification. Reported 96.7% appears to come from a held-out test set that likely shares subjects with training (subject-dependent identification), so it does not reflect leave-one-subject-out generalization to unseen people. Retrievable abstract lacks radar hardware parameters, exact window length, dataset size, split protocol, and per-subject metrics (full text paywalled). No cross-dataset or cross-session evaluation described in the abstract.
papers.relevance_to_us: Strongly relevant modality-wise: same radar micro-Doppler + deep-CNN pipeline we use for Parkinson's classification. Directly supports our design choice of feeding m-D spectrograms to a CNN and using transfer learning to cope with a small subject pool. However, the task differs fundamentally — this is a 20-class person-identification problem, whereas ours is binary PD-vs-control classification on 58 subjects with LOSO. Their evaluation is almost certainly subject-dependent (same people in train and test), which inflates accuracy relative to our cross-subject LOSO setting; their 96.7% is therefore not directly comparable to our ~0.62 LOSO AUC.
papers.lesson_for_us: (1) ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 fine-tuning is a validated, practical backbone for small radar micro-Doppler datasets — a reasonable transfer-learning baseline to try against our classical features. (2) Observation-window length is a first-class hyperparameter worth sweeping in our pipeline. (3) Most importantly, this paper illustrates the identification-vs-generalization gap: high accuracy from subject-dependent splits does not imply the model generalizes to unseen subjects. Our LOSO protocol is the more honest evaluation, and we should frame our lower-but-real PD signal accordingly and be cautious when citing such 90%+ radar-gait numbers, since they typically come from within-subject test splits, not cross-subject LOSO.
papers.evidence_quote: The gait dataset of 20 persons has been collected in an indoor environment where each subject was allowed to walk naturally and freely, which is absolutely more realistic and challenging than most existing works based on limited walking behaviour. Then, they perform identification using a transfer learned ResNet-50, which was fine-tuned on the gait m-D dataset based on the deep transfer learning technique. Through experiments, they first determined the optimal observation window length of m-D samples, and with this input, they achieved an average identification accuracy of 96.7% on the test set for 20 subjects, which highly outperforms the state-of-the-art methods.

papers.title: Parkinson's Disease Diagnosis and Severity Assessment from Gait Signals via Bayesian-Optimized Deep Learning
papers.authors: Mehmet Meral (Dept. of Neurosurgery, Private Erciyes Hospital, Kayseri, Turkey) and Ferdi Ozbilgin (Dept. of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, Giresun University, Turkey)
papers.venue: Diagnostics (MDPI, Basel), open access, Vol. 15, Issue 16, Article 2046. DOI: 10.3390/diagnostics15162046. Retrieved via PubMed Central open-access mirror (PMC12385253) because the MDPI page returned HTTP 403.
papers.modality: Wearable / force-sensing (NOT radar). Vertical Ground Reaction Force (VGRF) signals from instrumented insoles carrying eight force sensors under each foot (16 channels total), sampled at 100 Hz. This is a contact, foot-pressure modality — fundamentally different from contactless radar micro-Doppler.
papers.dataset: "Gait in Parkinson's Disease" (gaitpdb) database from PhysioNet (physionet.org/content/gaitpdb/1.0.0/). Pools three sub-studies: Yogev et al. (dual-task), Hausdorff et al. (rhythmic auditory stimulation/RAS), and Frenkel-Toledo et al. (treadmill).
papers.sample_size: 166 subjects total: 93 PD patients, 73 healthy controls. Hoehn–Yahr (HY) severity distribution: Stage 0 = 73, Stage 2 = 56, Stage 2.5 = 27, Stage 3 = 10 (heavily skewed toward mild/early stages; only 10 in Stage 3).
papers.methodology: End-to-end deep learning on raw VGRF signals, no manual feature engineering. Two architectures compared: a 1D CNN and an LSTM. Preprocessing = min-max normalization to [0,1]. Signals segmented into fixed-length windows of 5, 10, 15, 20, and 25 s. Hyperparameters tuned by Bayesian optimization (expected-improvement-plus acquisition, max 30 objective evaluations) using 5-fold cross-validation; search space included learning rate [1e-4, 1e-2], hidden units/filters [16-128], filter sizes [3-11], mini-batch size [16-128]. Final performance evaluated with 10-fold cross-validation stratified by diagnosis and HY stage. IMPORTANT: validation is segment/instance-level k-fold CV, described as subject-independent but NOT explicitly LOSO, and there is no external/independent-cohort test set — segments from one subject can plausibly land in both train and test folds.
papers.key_findings: Bayesian-optimized deep models on raw VGRF achieve very high accuracy for both PD detection (binary) and HY severity staging (multi-class). LSTM consistently outperformed CNN, attributed to better temporal-pattern capture. Performance stayed >90% across all window lengths; Bayesian optimization added roughly 1-2% accuracy over non-optimized baselines. Best binary result at the 10 s window; best staging result at the 5 s window.
papers.reported_performance: Binary PD-vs-control (LSTM, 10 s window): accuracy 99.42%, precision 99.42%, recall 99.42%, F1 99.42%, AUC 1.000. LSTM 5 s: 99.06% acc, AUC 1.000. Best CNN binary: 98.46% acc, AUC 0.998 (5 s). Multi-class HY staging (LSTM, 5 s): accuracy 98.24%, precision 97.47%, recall 98.25%, F1 97.85%, AUC 0.999; best CNN staging 96.62% acc, AUC 0.998 (5 s).
papers.pros: Non-invasive and low-cost (instrumented insoles); end-to-end pipeline removes hand-crafted feature engineering; robust across multiple temporal window sizes; principled hyperparameter tuning via Bayesian optimization gives a measurable gain; reports a full metric suite (accuracy/precision/recall/F1/AUC) for both tasks rather than accuracy alone; uses a well-known public benchmark (PhysioNet gaitpdb) aiding comparability.
papers.cons_limitations: Validated on a single public dataset with controlled recording conditions; the authors concede k-fold CV does not substitute for external validation on independent cohorts. No held-out subject-independent LOSO test is reported, so the near-ceiling (99%+, AUC 1.000) numbers are very likely optimistic due to possible per-subject segment leakage across folds. Severity classes are highly imbalanced (Stage 3 n=10), biasing multi-class results toward early stages. Only single-modality VGRF; real-world/free-living applicability untested. Future work: independent-cohort validation, hybrid CNN-LSTM, multi-sensor fusion, everyday-activity data, clinical validation.
papers.relevance_to_us: Moderately relevant as a comparison/contrast point, not a methodological twin. It shares the target task (PD detection + severity staging from gait) and the deep-learning-on-raw-signal philosophy (CNN/LSTM, Bayesian-optimized), which parallels our radar micro-Doppler CNN. But it differs on two axes that matter to us: (a) modality — contact VGRF insoles vs. our contactless radar micro-Doppler; and (b) validation rigor — it uses 5-/10-fold segment-level CV on 166 subjects with no LOSO and no external test, whereas we use subject-level LOSO on 58 subjects. Their 99%+ / AUC 1.000 figures sit far above our ~0.62 LOSO AUC, but the gap is largely an evaluation-protocol artifact: non-LOSO k-fold on segmented gait leaks subject identity and inflates scores. This paper is a good citation for "why LOSO matters" and for showing that headline gait-PD accuracies in the literature are often not subject-independent.
papers.lesson_for_us: Their near-perfect accuracy vs. our modest LOSO AUC is a protocol story, not a signal story: segment-level k-fold CV without subject partitioning inflates gait-PD performance because windows from the same person appear in both train and test. This directly validates our stricter LOSO design and confounds-control approach (duration-matched/residualized). Concretely: (1) cite this as an example of the leakage-prone evaluation we deliberately avoid; (2) borrow their good practices — Bayesian hyperparameter optimization and multi-window analysis (5-25 s) — which we could adopt for our radar CNN; (3) note their own admission that k-fold "does not substitute for external validation" to frame LOSO/subject-independent testing as the honest baseline for the field.
papers.evidence_quote: "The Bayesian-optimized LSTM achieved a peak binary classification accuracy of 99.42% with an AUC of 1.000 for PD versus control at the 10-s window, and 98.24% accuracy with an AUC of 0.999 for Hoehn–Yahr (HY) staging at the 5-s window." Also, on validation: "Although k-fold cross-validation mitigates overfitting within this cohort, it does not substitute for external validation on independent cohorts."

papers.title: Simulation study of deep-learning-based gait classification of young/elderly adults using Doppler radar
papers.authors: Toshiyuki Hoshiga, Kenshi Saho, Keitaro Shioiri, Masahiro Fujimoto, Yoshiyuki Kobayashi
papers.venue: Measurement: Sensors (Elsevier, open access), vol. 18, article no. 100103, December 2021. NOTE: The ScienceDirect full text returned HTTP 403; fields below are drawn from the abstract and bibliographic metadata as consistently rendered across multiple search sources (ScienceDirect listing, the Kenshi Saho lab publication page, and search-engine abstract summaries), not from the full PDF.
papers.modality: Radar — micro-Doppler / Doppler radar (MDR). Crucially, the radar signals were NOT measured but SIMULATED (synthesized) from optical motion-capture data of walking subjects; spectrograms (time-velocity distributions) were then computed from the simulated returns.
papers.dataset: An open optical motion-capture gait database (the AIST Gait Database, from AIST Japan; co-author Yoshiyuki Kobayashi is affiliated with AIST) used as the source of walking kinematics. Micro-Doppler radar returns were synthesized from these marker/segment trajectories. Task is a binary classification: young vs. elderly adults.
papers.sample_size: Not confirmable from the retrieved abstract. Search-engine summaries of this paper reference on the order of ~480 simulated micro-Doppler data samples generated from the AIST Gait Database for training/validation; the exact number of unique subjects was not stated in retrievable content. (Caution: a related but SEPARATE Saho study using real radar + LSTM used 300 subjects, 87 young + 213 elderly — do not attribute that number to this simulation paper.)
papers.methodology: Simulate micro-Doppler radar signatures from an open motion-capture gait dataset of young and elderly walkers (body-segment/point-scatterer style synthesis of the radar return from marker trajectories); compute time-velocity distribution (spectrogram) images from the simulated data; train a deep-learning image classifier on the spectrograms to distinguish young vs. elderly gait. Key experimental manipulation: repeat the classification using signals synthesized from different body-part subsets (whole body vs. legs only) to identify which body parts generate the most discriminative micro-Doppler data. The specific CNN architecture and the exact train/validation (cross-validation) protocol could not be confirmed from the retrieved abstract; no explicit leave-one-subject-out design was mentioned.
papers.key_findings: Classifying spectrograms synthesized from leg-only motion (thighs and shanks) is far more accurate than using whole-body signatures, i.e., the legs are the efficient target body parts for young/elderly gait discrimination. The study also demonstrates that motion-capture-driven simulation is a viable way to generate micro-Doppler radar training data for deep learning.
papers.reported_performance: Whole-body data: 74% classification accuracy. Leg-only (thigh + shank) data: 91% classification accuracy.
papers.pros: Contactless/remote sensing well suited to unobtrusive elderly monitoring; simulation-from-motion-capture enables controlled body-part ablation and cheap generation of labeled training data (mitigating scarce radar data); provides an actionable, interpretable insight (legs/lower limbs carry the discriminative signal); uses an open, reproducible motion-capture dataset; open-access publication.
papers.cons_limitations: Results are from SIMULATED, not measured, radar — a real-world sim-to-real gap is unaddressed (no experimental radar validation in this paper); the task is binary young vs. elderly (an age proxy), not a clinical disease such as Parkinson's; whole-body accuracy is only moderate (74%); the CNN architecture, exact sample/subject counts, and validation protocol are underspecified in retrievable content, and no subject-independent (LOSO) evaluation was confirmed, so reported accuracies may be optimistic; short-format article in a minor journal; the ScienceDirect full text was not directly accessible (HTTP 403), so methodological detail is limited to the abstract.
papers.relevance_to_us: High topical overlap with our work: micro-Doppler radar + spectrogram/time-velocity-distribution deep learning for a clinically-relevant gait population. Directly informs preprocessing/ROI choices for our PD CNN — it argues that isolating the lower-limb (thigh/shank) Doppler band, rather than the whole-body return, is where the discriminative gait information lives, which could raise our PD-vs-control accuracy. It also supports motion-capture-based MDR simulation as a data-augmentation strategy for a small cohort. Key differences from our setup: they classify young vs. elderly (not PD vs. control), use simulated (not real) radar, and do not use strict LOSO or 58 real subjects — so their numbers are not a like-for-like benchmark for our real-data, subject-independent task.
papers.lesson_for_us: (1) Try cropping/weighting our spectrograms to the leg velocity band (thigh/shank micro-Doppler) — this paper's jump from 74% (whole body) to 91% (legs only) suggests a large potential gain from lower-limb ROI selection. (2) Motion-capture-driven MDR simulation is a credible route to augment our scarce PD radar data. (3) Treat their 90%+ accuracy as an optimistic ceiling from simulated, non-subject-independent data; our LOSO-on-58-real-subjects protocol is harder and more honest, consistent with our observed weaker-but-real signal, so we should not expect simulation-level accuracy and should keep our confound-controlled, subject-independent evaluation.
papers.evidence_quote: the classification rate using whole-body data was 74%, however, using only leg data showed an accuracy of 91%, which indicates that the thighs and shanks are efficient target body parts for the gait classification of both young and elderly adults

papers.title: Micro-Doppler Based Classification of Human Aquatic Activities via Transfer Learning of Convolutional Neural Networks
papers.authors: Jinhee Park, Rios Jesus Javier, Taesup Moon, Youngwook Kim
papers.modality: Radar (Doppler radar micro-Doppler signatures). Continuous-wave Doppler radar at 7.25 GHz, 15 dBm output power, vertical polarization. Spectrograms generated via STFT.
papers.dataset: Custom-collected dataset of micro-Doppler spectrograms of five human aquatic activities recorded in a controlled swimming pool. Activities: freestyle swimming, backstroke, breaststroke, swimming while pulling a floating boat, and rowing. Spectrograms produced by STFT (FFT size 256, non-overlapping 20 ms step), Doppler range 0-500 Hz, final image size 252 x 100 pixels.
papers.sample_size: 5 human subjects (avg height 178 cm, weight 76 kg); 5 activity classes; 625 total spectrogram samples (5 measurements per subject per activity, 5 spectrograms per measurement at 2-second intervals = 25 samples per activity per subject).
papers.methodology: Compared four deep CNN configurations against a handcrafted-feature SVM baseline. (1) DCNN-Scratch-I: 3 conv layers (20 filters, 5x5), ReLU, 2x2 max pooling, ~4M params, trained from scratch. (2) DCNN-Scratch-II: consecutive conv filters before pooling, ~55M params, from scratch. (3) DCNN-TL-AlexNet: ImageNet-pretrained AlexNet (5 conv + 3 FC, ~60M params) fine-tuned on spectrograms. (4) DCNN-TL-VGG16: ImageNet-pretrained VGG16 (13 conv + 3 FC, 138M params) fine-tuned. Transfer learning takes networks pre-trained on RGB ImageNet and fine-tunes on the radar spectrogram data. Baseline: SVM with 8 handcrafted micro-Doppler features and a Gaussian kernel; missing/unmeasurable features imputed with activity/subject averages. Training: mini-batch SGD with momentum 0.9, batch size 50, dropout 0.5 at FC layer, up to 5000 iterations, learning rates 0.01 / 0.0005 / 0.001 / 0.0005 respectively. Validation: 5-fold cross-validation with each fold being data from one subject (i.e., a leave-one-subject-out scheme).
papers.key_findings: Deep CNNs learn features automatically from raw spectrograms and outperform handcrafted-feature SVM even when trained from scratch on only 625 samples. Transfer learning from ImageNet-pretrained networks gives the largest gain: low-level features (edges, textures) learned on natural RGB images generalize effectively to micro-Doppler spectrograms. The pre-trained VGG16 was both the most accurate and the fastest to converge (~100 SGD iterations vs. ~400 for the from-scratch model). Aquatic micro-Doppler signatures are noisier and lower-RCS than dry-ground activities, making the problem harder.
papers.reported_performance: 5-fold (per-subject) cross-validation classification accuracy: SVM handcrafted features 45.1%; DCNN-Scratch-I 61.9%; DCNN-Scratch-II 66.7%; DCNN-TL-AlexNet 74.6%; DCNN-TL-VGG16 80.3% (best). The transfer-learned VGG16 represents roughly a 78% relative improvement over the SVM baseline; it also converged in ~100 SGD iterations versus ~400 for the from-scratch DCNN.
papers.pros: Automatic feature learning eliminates handcrafted feature engineering. Transfer learning delivers strong accuracy despite a very small dataset (625 samples, 5 subjects). Demonstrates that ImageNet low-level features transfer to radar spectrograms. Radar works in all weather and lighting conditions. Clear, well-controlled ablation comparing from-scratch vs. transfer-learned and two backbone depths, with a fair handcrafted-feature baseline.
papers.cons_limitations: Very small dataset (5 subjects, 625 samples) limits from-scratch training and generalization claims. Data collected in a controlled swimming pool; authors note ocean waves would substantially degrade performance. Aquatic signatures are noisy with low human RCS (water drops, waves), reducing discriminability. Handcrafted baseline weakened by unmeasurable features requiring average-imputation, which may understate the classical approach. Only 5 subjects means the per-subject cross-validation has high variance and limited statistical power. Best accuracy (80.3%) still modest in absolute terms.
papers.relevance_to_us: Highly relevant. This is a radar micro-Doppler + CNN classification study on spectrogram images, the same signal/model family as our radar micro-Doppler Parkinson's CNN. Most directly, their validation uses 5-fold cross-validation where each fold is one subject, i.e. a leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) protocol like ours (though only 5 subjects vs. our 58). It provides direct precedent for treating spectrograms as images and fine-tuning ImageNet-pretrained backbones (AlexNet, VGG16) on small radar datasets, and quantifies the transfer-learning gain over both from-scratch CNNs and a handcrafted-feature SVM baseline (comparable to our classical baseline).
papers.lesson_for_us: On small radar micro-Doppler datasets, fine-tuning an ImageNet-pretrained CNN (VGG16 here) can substantially beat both from-scratch CNNs and handcrafted-feature classifiers, and converges faster — a strong argument for trying transfer learning against our classical LOSO baseline (~0.62 AUC). It also validates evaluating per-subject (LOSO) to avoid subject leakage. Caveats to carry over: with few subjects, per-subject CV is noisy, so our 58-subject LOSO gives far more reliable estimates; and, as our duration-confound work shows, we must ensure any deep-learning gain reflects real physiology rather than an incidental confound (their handcrafted baseline was also weakened by feature imputation, a reminder to keep baselines fair).
papers.evidence_quote: The transfer learned DCNN, which takes a DCNN pre-trained on a RGB image dataset and fine-tunes the parameters using the collected data, achieves a much higher 80.3%, which is a significant performance boost.

papers.title: Motion Classification using Kinematically Sifted ACGAN-Synthesized Radar Micro-Doppler Signatures
papers.authors: Baris Erol, Sevgi Zubeyde Gurbuz, Moeness G. Amin
papers.venue: arXiv preprint (eess.SP, arXiv:2001.08582, 19 Jan 2020); accepted to IEEE Transactions on Aerospace and Electronic Systems
papers.modality: Radar micro-Doppler. Continuous-wave (CW) radar transmitting at 25 GHz, 10 ms sweep time, 128 samples/sweep, oversampled at 12.8 kHz then downsampled to 1.2 kHz. Signals converted to STFT spectrograms (window length 512, overlap 256), then to grayscale and resized to 100x100x1 before input to the generative models and CNN.
papers.dataset: Two self-collected datasets at Villanova University. (1) Line-of-sight (LOS) dataset from the Radar Imaging Laboratory: 8 activities at aspect angles 0/30/45 deg and 3 speeds (slow/typical/fast); 1586 samples. Per-class LOS counts: bending 167, falling 350, kneeling 216, gesture 150, reaching 140, sitting 233, standing 130, walking 200. Used to train the ACGAN. (2) Through-the-wall radar (TWR) dataset from the Center for Advanced Communications conference room: subject behind a plywood wall, starting 5 m away, moving toward/away from radar; aspect angles 0/30/45/60 deg; 387 samples (bending 50, falling 72, gesture 50, kneeling 15, reaching 50, sitting 50, standing 50, walking 50). Used only as the cross-environment test set. (Note: the LOS/TWR location labels appear swapped between the prose and Table I.)
papers.sample_size: Training (LOS): 14 human participants (12 male, 2 female), heights 5.1-6.3 ft, weights 119-220 lbs; 1586 real spectrograms. Test (TWR): 1 male subject who was NOT part of the LOS collection; 387 real spectrograms. ACGAN then generates a large synthetic training set from the LOS data.
papers.methodology: Physics-informed GAN data augmentation for radar human activity recognition to overcome small radar training sets.
